target.title: feat(config): add compaction.thinkingLevel to override thinking level during compaction
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Compaction always shares the session's current thinking level. There is no way to independently control thinking behavior during compaction summarization. Users who want to save tokens/cost during compaction or avoid thinking artifacts in summaries had no option to disable thinking for compaction alone.

This adds `agents.defaults.compaction.thinkingLevel` config option. When set, compaction uses this thinking level instead of the session's current level. Precedence: `config.compaction.thinkingLevel` > inherited session `thinkLevel` > `"off"` (default).

## Evidence

Proxy log comparison — same session, before and after setting `compaction.thinkingLevel`.

**Before** — session thinking = `"high"`, `compaction.thinkingLevel` unset — compaction request passes `thinking: "high"`, response includes `reasoning_content`:

```
Request 903:
{
  "model": "Qwen3.6-27B-FP8",
  "thinking": { "enabled": true, "level": "high" },
  "stream": true,
  ...
}

Response 903:
{
  "choices": [{
    "delta": {
      "reasoning_content": "thinking block content...",
    }
  }]
}
```

**After** — same session, set `compaction.thinkingLevel: "off"` — compaction request omits thinking, response has no `reasoning_content`:

```
Request 907:
{
  "model": "Qwen3.6-27B-FP8",
  "stream": true,
  "stream_options": {
    "include_usage": true
  },
  "max_completion_tokens": 16000
}

Response:
{
  "id": "chatcmpl-986428eb-dc58-4a7d-bc2d-881504084088",
  "choices": [{
    "index": 0,
    "delta": {
      "role": "assistant",
      "content": "...compaction summary...",
      "reasoning_content": null,
      "tool_calls": null
    },
    "finish_reason": "stop"
  }],
  "usage": {
    "prompt_tokens": 289,
    "total_tokens": 648,
    "completion_tokens": 359
  }
}
```

Key observations:
- Same session, same model, same compaction trigger — only the config changed
- **Before**: request 903 — `thinking: { enabled: true, level: "high" }` → `reasoning_content` present (~2-3K thinking tokens)
- **After**: request 907 — no thinking param → `reasoning_content: null` (359 completion tokens, no thinking overhead)
- Token count drops significantly when thinking is disabled via config

## Verification

- Unit tests pass (12 new/updated tests across 3 test files)
  - `config.compaction-settings.test.ts` (9 tests) — config parsing
  - `compact.thinking.test.ts` (6 tests) — thinkLevel precedence rules
  - `schema.help.quality.test.ts` (23 tests) — help/label coverage
- Config schema validates all 8 ThinkLevel values
- Embedded-agent-runner (`compact.ts`) reads `compaction.thinkingLevel` with correct precedence
- Codex native compaction warns that `compaction.thinkingLevel` is ignored (no-op scoped)
- Schema labels and help text updated

## Files Changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/config/zod-schema.agent-defaults.ts` | Add `thinkingLevel` to compaction zod schema |
| `src/config/types.agent-defaults.ts` | Add `thinkingLevel` to `AgentCompactionConfig`, dedupe `provider` |
| `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact.ts` | Read `compaction.thinkingLevel` from config as fallback |
| `src/agents/sessions/agent-session.ts` | Add `compactionThinkingLevel` option to `runCompactionWork` |
| `src/config/schema.labels.ts` | Add label for `compaction.thinkingLevel` |
| `src/config/schema.help.ts` | Add help text |
| `src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts` | Add key + enum expectations |
| `src/config/config.compaction-settings.test.ts` | 4 new config parsing tests |
| `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact.thinking.test.ts` | 6 new precedence tests |

## Compatibility / Migration

- **Backward compatible**: unset config preserves existing behavior
- **New optional field only**, no migration needed

target.title: fix(agents): count CJK tool-result text by token-equivalent length
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: The live per-turn tool-result truncation cap converts token budgets to character budgets with a flat 4-chars-per-token heuristic but measured tool-result text with raw UTF-16 `text.length`. A result made mostly of CJK text was accepted under the cap while its real token count was up to 4x the budget the cap exists to enforce.

**Solution**: Keep `toolResultMaxChars` as an independent **physical** UTF-16 ceiling and add a separate **token-equivalent** budget (the 30% context-share limit) measured with the existing CJK-aware `estimateStringChars` helper. The complete retained result must satisfy BOTH limits.

**What changed**: `getToolResultTextLength` stays a raw measurement (physical cap); a new `getToolResultEstimatedTextLength` measures token-equivalent length. `truncateToolResultText` gates on both budgets and re-checks the fully assembled prefix/tail/marker/suffix against the estimated budget, shrinking Unicode-safely. Plus tests and a docs note.

**What did NOT change**: The estimated budget is opt-in, so the persistence guard keeps its physical-only cap and pure ASCII behavior is byte-for-byte identical. The `maxChars` formula, the `toolResultMaxChars` config contract, and the output format are unchanged.

Fixes #103847

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: `calculateMaxToolResultCharsWithCap` derives a token budget (`maxTokens * 4`) but the truncation compared/sliced against it using raw `text.length`. For CJK text (encoded at ~1 token/char, not ~1 token/4 chars) a 16000-char result reported 16000 against a 16000 cap and was never truncated, while its real cost was ~16000 tokens.

**Why This Change Was Made**: A maintainer's prior decision on this issue defined a two-budget contract — keep the configured cap as a physical UTF-16 ceiling and enforce a separate token-derived budget. This PR implements exactly that, reusing `estimateStringChars` (already used by `preemptive-compaction.ts`, `pruner.ts`, and `openai-transport-stream.ts`) rather than reinterpreting the physical config ceiling as a CJK-weighted one.

**User Impact**: CJK-heavy tool results are bounded to their real share of the context window without over-truncating results that already fit both budgets. ASCII/Latin content and the physical `toolResultMaxChars` ceiling are unaffected.

## Root Cause

**Trigger condition**: A tool result whose text is dense CJK (or other non-Latin) content whose raw UTF-16 length fits the physical cap but whose token-equivalent length exceeds the context-share budget.

**Root cause analysis**: The physical cap and the token budget were collapsed into one number and measured with raw `text.length`, so CJK content bypassed the token budget. A whole-input inflation ratio also cannot bound a compositionally different retained slice.

**Affected scope**: `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.ts` — the live tool-result truncation path wired into `run.ts`, `run/attempt.ts`, and `session-tool-result-guard.ts`.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Enforce a separate token-equivalent budget on the actual retained tool-result text while keeping `toolResultMaxChars` a physical UTF-16 ceiling.

**Real environment tested**: Linux 4.19.112-2.el8.x86_64, Node.js 22.x, OpenClaw main @ 7ac8e2e227, real exported functions driven directly via `node --import tsx` (not mocked).

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

Drive the real exported functions with the mixed-script counterexample and the physical-cap / live-path cases:
```bash
node --import tsx -e "
import { truncateToolResultText, truncateOversizedToolResultsInMessages } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.js';
import { estimateStringChars } from './src/utils/cjk-chars.js';
const mixed = '字'.repeat(5000) + 'a'.repeat(15000);
const r = truncateToolResultText(mixed, 1000000, { estimatedMaxChars: 16000 });
console.log('mixed retained est', estimateStringChars(r), '<=16000', estimateStringChars(r) <= 16000);
const cjk8k = [{ role: 'toolResult', content: [{ type: 'text', text: '字'.repeat(8000) }], id: 'a', timestamp: 1, toolCallId: 't' }];
console.log('8000 CJK truncatedCount', truncateOversizedToolResultsInMessages(cjk8k, 50000).truncatedCount);
"
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
== P1-2 mixed-script counterexample (old code emitted ~24142) ==
input estimated: 35000
retained estimated: 15781 | <= 16000: true

== P1-1 physical cap NOT CJK-weighted: 8000 CJK, physical 16000, ctx 50000 ==
truncatedCount: 0 (0 = not over-truncated)

== live path bounds large CJK to 30% token share ==
truncatedCount: 1 | retained est: 59781 | <= E(60000): true

== ASCII unchanged ==
8000 ASCII truncatedCount: 0 (0)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: The mixed-script counterexample (CJK-heavy prefix + ASCII tail) retains 15781 estimated chars — within the 16000 budget — because the actual retained text is measured, not a whole-input average. An 8000-char CJK result that fits both budgets is not truncated (physical cap is not CJK-weighted). A 30000-char CJK result is bounded to 59781 estimated chars (the 30% share of a 50K context). ASCII is unchanged.

**What was not tested**: I did not run against a real provider tokenizer (no tokenizer library is bundled); the estimate uses the codebase's own `estimateStringChars`, already relied on in four sibling paths as the corrected estimate for this undercount class.

## Tests and validation

### Unit tests

```
pnpm test -- src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  73 passed (73)
   Duration  5.81s
```

Adds two-budget coverage: physical/estimated separation, the mixed-script overflow counterexample, CJK Extension B surrogate safety, and live-path integration (configured-cap no-op, large-CJK share bound, mixed-script, 50K/128K tiers). Related suites pass unchanged (`session-tool-result-guard` 35, `preemptive-compaction` 22). Also validated with `pnpm tsgo:core` (clean) and oxlint (clean).

## Linked context

- **Issue**: #103847
- **Related PRs**: #104055 (competing candidate for the same issue), #103901 (earlier attempt, closed after the two-budget design was defined)
- **In scope**: Per-result live truncation two-budget enforcement in `tool-result-truncation.ts`
- **Out of scope**: The separate aggregate tool-result budget (kept on its existing raw measurement)

## Risk checklist

merge-risk: Low

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — ASCII behavior is byte-for-byte identical; the physical `toolResultMaxChars` ceiling is unchanged
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations — all 73 tests pass, config contract unchanged
- [x] No breaking changes — estimated budget is opt-in; persistence guard stays physical-only
- [x] Mitigation: reuses the already-tested shared `estimateStringChars` helper; the retained result is verified against both budgets
- [x] Documentation updated — `docs/reference/token-use.md` describes the physical ceiling plus the separate token-share guard

target.title: fix(azure): responses model aliases route correctly
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users configuring `azure-openai-responses/*` could have model status probes and embedded-agent runs resolve through the OpenAI owner/auth path instead of the configured Azure Responses credentials and base URL.

The inverse boundary also matters: OpenAI-owned, manifest-suppressed models such as `gpt-5.3-codex-spark` must still produce the OpenAI OAuth remediation instead of being misclassified as an Azure deployment.

Closes #93781

## Why This Change Was Made

Alias canonicalization now considers the requested model together with configured Azure endpoint/model surface and manifest suppressions before choosing the provider owner. Configured Azure models and custom deployments keep `azure-openai-responses`; endpoint-less aliases and unconditionally suppressed OpenAI models canonicalize to `openai`.

Conditional suppressions do not rewrite alias ownership at this earlier stage, even when their endpoint condition matches. Their `when.baseUrlHosts` and `when.providerConfigApiIn` policy remains with the existing runtime suppression evaluator, so an alias does not lose its endpoint or credential owner before that policy is evaluated.

Configured overrides also carry the requested provider onto discovered model rows, so Azure API/base URL/auth ownership is preserved after catalog lookup. This does not change public config, schema, migrations, credential storage, or the OpenAI plugin manifest.

When an Azure provider config supplies its endpoint and credential but omits the optional `api` field, the resolver consumes the transport API declared by the retained manifest alias before discovered OpenAI metadata. It does not infer an API from arbitrary provider ids, so params-only GitHub Copilot configurations keep their discovered per-model protocols.

## User Impact

Azure Responses users can probe and run configured `azure-openai-responses` models without OpenClaw silently switching to an OpenAI auth profile. Provider-level Azure deployment names remain Azure-owned, Codex-only models continue to point users to the correct OpenAI OAuth flow, and GitHub Copilot Enterprise params-only configs retain Anthropic/OpenAI transports selected per model.

## Evidence

- Rebuilt the branch on the pinned current-main snapshot `6de8aa6f9b750ebfcdc15048090b62076f19197e` and removed the merge commit `56d6c3b8e662c127315921979d794816bc6ec7b6`. The 14 original contribution commits were replayed linearly with their original authors, leaving zero merge commits in the contribution range.
- Before the follow-up repair below, the history port was byte-for-byte equivalent to the hosted diff (`40b07ded6d508b744a6a039bfa3e2e1494b7cc8e230b62bf8f0b1c4d03aaac1b`) and `git range-diff` matched all 14 original contribution commits. Exact-head review then found that conditional suppression declarations were being consumed as unconditional owner overrides; the candidate adds one bounded production/test repair for that finding.
- Focused resolver regression suite:

  ```text
  Test Files  3 passed (3)
  Tests       197 passed (197)
  ```

  The suite includes discovered and configured-fallback Azure cases with `baseUrl` configured and `api` omitted; a retained manifest alias carrying both `api` and `baseUrl`; a retained alias with no provider config; and params-only GitHub Copilot Claude, Gemini, and GPT cases. Azure resolves to `azure-openai-responses`; Copilot retains `anthropic-messages`, `openai-completions`, and `openai-responses` respectively.

  It also verifies the trust boundary around manifest aliases: inactive workspace claims are ignored, external claims must be explicitly activated/trusted, config-load-path owners retain their operator-granted trust, and multiple eligible owners claiming the same alias fail closed instead of combining one plugin's provider with another plugin's transport metadata. A call-count regression confirms each async model lookup prepares alias owner/transport metadata once rather than rescanning it at three resolver seams.

  The regression matrix also verifies that an explicit Azure model row cannot override unconditional manifest suppression for `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`; the resolver keeps the OpenAI owner and returns the Codex OAuth remediation. Owner-boundary cases prove that conditional suppressions do not canonicalize a transport alias for either matching or non-matching configured endpoints, while an unconditional suppression still canonicalizes it.

- A CI follow-up deduplicated repeated alias-resolution assertions in `model.static-catalog.test.ts` after the repository `max-lines` rule flagged that PR-owned test file. The exact candidate passes the complete file (`28 passed`), changed-file lint including `max-lines`, formatting, and `git diff --check`; production behavior and coverage are unchanged.
- The same remote run also reported an unrelated UI import cycle, stale bundled-channel metadata, deprecated plugin-SDK usage, and additional lint findings in base-owned files outside this PR diff. `openclaw/ci-gate` only aggregates those failed children; this PR does not modify those baseline files.
- Formatting, changed-file lint, `git diff --check`, and the current-main `max-lines` ratchet passed. The ratchet ran on the exact synthetic PR merge preview and accepted the changed production/test surface without adding or expanding a baseline entry.
- No local typecheck claim is made for this candidate. The protected `check:test-types` lane was not started because this host uses cgroup v1 and cannot attest the required `memory.high` envelope; hosted CI remains the full typecheck gate.
- A fresh credential-free production resolver/dispatch driver observed:

  ```json
  {
    "azure": { "provider": "azure-openai-responses", "api": "azure-openai-responses", "baseUrl": "https://example.openai.azure.com/openai/v1", "transport": "openclaw-azure-openai-responses-transport" },
    "azureCustomDeployment": { "provider": "azure-openai-responses", "api": "azure-openai-responses", "baseUrl": "https://example.openai.azure.com/openai/v1", "transport": "openclaw-azure-openai-responses-transport" },
    "copilotClaude": { "provider": "github-copilot", "api": "anthropic-messages", "transport": "openclaw-anthropic-messages-transport" },
    "copilotGemini": { "provider": "github-copilot", "api": "openai-completions", "transport": "openclaw-openai-completions-transport" },
    "copilotGpt": { "provider": "github-copilot", "api": "openai-responses", "transport": "openclaw-openai-responses-transport" }
  }
  ```

- The existing PR proof ran the real `openclaw models status --probe --probe-provider azure-openai-responses` CLI path against a local Responses-compatible endpoint. It observed `azure-openai-responses/gpt-5.5`, the configured Azure-style URL, and `api-key` rather than `Authorization`; ClawSweeper marked that proof sufficient.

target.title: fix(ui): prevent CLS on chat images with min-height placeholder
target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Chat messages containing images cause **Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)** during image loading. Before the image finishes downloading, the `` element has zero height (no `width`/`height` attributes on seven of the ten image-extraction paths). Once loaded, the image suddenly expands to its rendered size (up to 300×200 px), pushing all messages below it downward. On slow connections, users reading content immediately below an image see it jump away mid-reading. The previous PR iteration used `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2`. Missing the `auto` keyword means the **explicit ratio remains the preferred box ratio even after the image loads** (CSS Sizing spec §6.1). Portrait images (e.g. 200×300, 2:3) and square images (e.g. 300×300, 1:1) are permanently forced into a 3:2 outer box, with `object-fit: contain` producing visible letterboxing. The image never recovers its natural shape. ## Why This Change Was Made Use `aspect-ratio: auto 3 / 2`: - **Before load**: the browser reserves a 3:2 box (matching `max-width: 300px` / `max-height: 200px`). Downstream content stays anchored — no CLS. - **After load**: `auto` tells the browser "if this replaced element has intrinsic dimensions, use those." The image recovers its natural aspect ratio. A portrait image displays at 2:3, a square at 1:1, a 3:2 at 3:2. Without `auto`: - `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2` sets the **preferred** aspect ratio. Per the CSS Sizing specification, a replaced element's natural dimensions do NOT override the preferred ratio — only the `auto` keyword creates a fallback behavior where intrinsic dimensions win. - Portrait, square, and dimension-attributed images are permanently locked in a 3:2 box. `object-fit: contain` adds letterboxing inside that box. With `auto 3 / 2`: - The 3:2 ratio is a **fallback** used only when no intrinsic dimensions are available (before load, or for images that never provide dimensions). - Once the image loads, natural dimensions take over. ## User Impact - Messages below images stay anchored during loading (3:2 placeholder). - After load, every image displays at its natural aspect ratio (no forced 3:2 letterboxing for portrait or square images). - The muted background (`var(--bg-muted)`) remains as a visual loading indicator. ## Evidence ### Standalone HTML proof — `auto 3/2` vs `3/2` across ratios A standalone HTML page (`/tmp/aspect-ratio-auto-proof.html`) renders identical 3:2, 2:3 (portrait), and 1:1 (square) images under the two CSS rules plus a delayed-load CLS measurement with red reference lines. ``` Rule A: aspect-ratio: 3 / 2 (no auto) 3:2 image (300×200) → OK: matches placeholder 2:3 portrait (200×300) → ❌ forced into 3:2 box — letterboxed 1:1 square (300×300) → ❌ forced into 3:2 box — letterboxed Rule B: aspect-ratio: auto 3 / 2 (with auto) 3:2 image (300×200) → ✅ natural 3:2 recovered 2:3 portrait (200×300) → ✅ natural 2:3 recovered 1:1 square (300×300) → ✅ natural 1:1 recovered Rule C: delayed-load + auto 3/2 (CLS measurement) 3:2 image → ref shift: 0.0px ✅ (placeholder = final size) portrait → ref shift: 0.0px ✅ (auto yields to natural ratio) square → ref shift: 0.0px ✅ (auto yields to natural ratio) ``` The HTML proof is self-contained and can be opened in any browser to verify the three rules above. ### CSS spec citation — why `auto` is required CSS Sizing Module Level 3, §6.1: > `aspect-ratio: auto 3 / 2` — If the element has a natural aspect ratio, use that. Otherwise, use 3/2. > `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2` — The preferred aspect ratio is always 3/2, regardless of natural dimensions. Without `auto`, the explicit ratio wins over intrinsic dimensions. With `auto`, intrinsic dimensions win over the fallback. ### Build proof ``` $ node scripts/ui.js build ✓ built in 6.10s ``` Compiled CSS confirms `aspect-ratio:auto 3/2`: ``` chat-message-image{border-radius:var(--radius-md);object-fit:contain; aspect-ratio:auto 3/2;background:var(--bg-muted); max-width:300px;max-height:200px;transition:transform .15s ease-out} ``` **Observed result**: Images now receive a 3:2 placeholder before load (preventing CLS), then recover their natural aspect ratio after load (no permanent letterboxing). **What was not tested**: A real Control UI browser session with delayed images of different ratios. The standalone HTML proof demonstrates the identical CSS rules on real `` elements with the same `max-width`/`max-height`/`object-fit` constraints used in `.chat-message-image`. The browser rendering engine is the same. ## Regression Test Plan ``` $ node scripts/ui.js build ✓ built in 6.10s $ git diff --stat upstream/main.. ui/src/styles/chat/layout.css | 19 ++++++++++++------- 1 file changed, 12 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-) ``` Net change: +5 lines of comments, +2 characters in the rule (`auto `). No runtime logic changed. The CSS addition only affects the computed dimensions of `` elements with class `.chat-message-image`. ## Root Cause `.chat-message-image` had `max-width: 300px` and `max-height: 200px` without any spatial reservation, causing the browser to collapse the element to 0×0 before load. The `min-height: 40px` fix in the original PR provided a nonzero minimum but left up to 160 px of residual CLS. The `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2` fix reserved correct space but trapped non-3:2 images in a permanent 3:2 outer box. The CSS Sizing specification requires the `auto` keyword for a fallback ratio: `aspect-ratio: auto 3 / 2` means "use the natural ratio if available, otherwise fall back to 3/2." Without `auto`, `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2` is a fixed preferred ratio — the element's natural dimensions never override it. ## AI Assistance CSS analysis, `auto` keyword fix, standalone HTML proof, and this PR body were drafted with agent assistance. All build commands were run locally.

target.title: fix(sessions-send): normalize sourceSessionKey to dmScope-resolved canonical key
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `session.dmScope` is `"main"` (default), inter-agent messages sent via `sessions_send` embed the calling session persisted storage key as `sourceSessionKey` — even when that key was created under a previous `per-account-channel-peer` routing regime. The receiving agent replies to the stale key, creating a ghost session that the sender never monitors, causing permanent one-way communication failure between agents.

**Split path:**
1. **Inbound user DMs** → resolved via `buildAgentPeerSessionKey()` with `dmScope="main"` → lands in `agent:{id}:main` ✓
2. **Inter-session replies** → routed to `sourceSessionKey` from provenance → lands in `agent:{id}:{channel}:{account}:direct:{peer}` (stale format) ✗

Two different session keys → two different sessions → the agent in session A never sees replies delivered to session B.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `sessions_send` tool passed `opts.agentSessionKey` verbatim into `inputProvenance.sourceSessionKey`. This is the session persisted key from storage, not a dmScope-resolved key. The fix normalizes the requester key through `buildAgentMainSessionKey()` when `dmScope` is `"main"`, so all downstream provenance, watch registration, same-session detection, and A2A ping-pong routing use the same canonical key that the agent actually monitors.

## User Impact

Multi-agent setups using `dmScope="main"` (the default) with sessions that predate a routing regime change will now correctly route inter-agent replies back to the sender monitored session. No config changes required. Operators with `dmScope` set to `per-peer`, `per-channel-peer`, or `per-account-channel-peer` are unaffected — the normalization only activates when `dmScope` is `"main"`.

## Evidence

- `sessions-send-helpers.test.ts`: **10/10 passed**
- `sessions-send-tool.a2a.test.ts`: **25/25 passed**
- oxfmt and git diff --check clean

Fixes #107399

target.title: fix(cron): anchor regex patterns with ^...$ for llama.cpp JSON Schema compatibility
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The cron tool and gateway-protocol schemas use unanchored `pattern: "\S"` (at least one non-whitespace character). This is valid JSON Schema but **rejected by llama.cpp**'s JSON Schema parser, which requires regex patterns to start with `^` and end with `$`.

Affected users cannot use the built-in cron tool with llama.cpp-based backends (LM Studio, llama-swap, LiteLLM→llama.cpp). The error is:
```
Unable to generate parser for this template.
Pattern must start with '^' and end with '$'
```

This is a **regression** from 2026.6.11 → 2026.7.1. Fixes #107449. Also reported as #107824.

## Evidence

All 5 pattern locations in 4 files changed from `\S` to `^.*\S.*$` (identical semantics — "at least one non-whitespace character" — with proper anchors).

target.title: fix(mcp): normalize disabled:true to enabled:false in canonicalizeConfiguredMcpServer
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #103954 — MCP `disabled: true` was silently ignored. When a user set `mcp.servers.<name>.disabled: true` in `openclaw.json`, the gateway still spawned MCP server processes (e.g. `claude mcp serve`) because:

1. The `McpServerSchema` only defined `enabled`, not `disabled`
2. `.catchall(z.unknown())` silently accepted `disabled: true` without any effect
3. All runtime checks use `enabled === false`, so the `disabled` flag was never consumed

The only workaround was to delete the server entry entirely with `openclaw mcp unset <name>`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two changes, following the existing canonicalization pattern:

1. **`canonicalizeConfiguredMcpServer()`** — Normalizes `disabled: true` → `enabled: false` when `enabled` is not already explicitly set. This mirrors the existing pattern of mapping legacy snake_case keys to canonical camelCase fields (`type` → `transport`, `connect_timeout` → `connectTimeout`, etc.). If both `enabled` and `disabled` are present, `enabled` wins.

2. **`McpServerSchema`** — Adds `disabled: z.boolean().optional()` so it is explicitly parsed by zod rather than silently swallowed by catchall.

## User Impact

Users who set `mcp.servers.<name>.disabled: true` will now have the server properly excluded from runtime (no process spawned, not probed, not included in tool catalogs). The existing `enabled: false` workflow continues to work identically.

## Evidence

- **New tests** (`src/config/mcp-config-normalize.test.ts`): 5 test cases covering:
  - `disabled: true` → `enabled: false`
  - Existing `enabled: false` unchanged
  - `disabled: true` does not overwrite explicit `enabled: true`
  - `disabled: false` is a no-op
  - Servers without `disabled` pass through unchanged
- **Existing tests all pass** (88 MCP-related tests across 6 test files, no regressions):
  - `src/config/mcp-config.test.ts` — 8 tests
  - `src/agents/bundle-mcp-config.test.ts` — 4 tests

target.title: fix(cli): restore terminal state before exit in logs and hooks commands
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`process.exit(1)` in `logs-cli.ts:685` and `hooks-cli.ts:153` bypasses the CLI's standard exit path (`runtime.exit()`), which calls `restoreTerminalState()` before terminating. This means the terminal state (raw mode, cursor visibility, ANSI reset sequences, active progress line) is not cleaned up when these commands exit on error.

Additionally, the hooks-cli replacement (`defaultRuntime.exit(1)`) breaks the `never` type contract because `defaultRuntime.exit()` returns `void`, not `never`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Every other CLI command uses `runtime.exit()` → `restoreTerminalState()` → `process.exit()` as defined in `src/runtime.ts:89-96`. These two call sites were the only exceptions.

This revision routes both error paths through the canonical `defaultRuntime.exit(1)`:
- **hooks-cli.ts**: Added `throw new Error("unreachable")` after `defaultRuntime.exit(1)` — matches the same pattern in `src/runtime.ts:94` that preserves the `never` return type contract and satisfies tests when `process.exit` is mocked
- **logs-cli.ts**: Replaced manual `restoreTerminalState()` + `process.exit(1)` with `defaultRuntime.exit(1)`, eliminating the duplicated cleanup and the now-unused `restoreTerminalState` import

## User Impact

Very low in practice — `logs follow` does not set raw mode itself, and `restoreTerminalState()` operations all have TTY guards. But it is a defensive fix to ensure terminal state is always restored on exit, consistent with the rest of the CLI contract.

## Evidence

- **Contract**: `src/runtime.ts:89-96` — `defaultRuntime.exit()` calls `restoreTerminalState("runtime exit", ...)` before `process.exit()`
- **Consistency**: All other CLI commands (config, plugins-search, devices, gateway run-loop) use `runtime.exit()`
- **Commit history**: `git blame` confirms the raw `process.exit(1)` was added in the initial monorepo import commit with no subsequent discussion or adjustment

### Tests
- `pnpm test src/cli/hooks-cli.test.ts` — 5/5 passed
- `pnpm test src/cli/logs-cli.test.ts` — 37/37 passed
- `pnpm tsgo:core` — passed (prod type check)
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test` — passed (test type check)
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint` — clean
- `pnpm format:check` — passed

### Real Behavior Proof

**Setup**: Built CLI from branch (`1d76252`), ran inside a PTY (`script -q -c "..." /dev/null`) so `process.stdin.isTTY=true` and `process.stdout.isTTY=true`, ensuring all `restoreTerminalState()` code paths execute.

`restoreTerminalState()` in `packages/terminal-core/src/restore.ts` does four things on TTY:
1. `clearActiveProgressLine()` — clears any active progress line
2. `stdin.setRawMode(false)` — exits raw mode if previously set
3. `process.stdout.write(RESET_SEQUENCE)` — sends the ANSI escape sequence:
   `\x1b[0m\x1b[?25h\x1b[?1000l\x1b[?1002l\x1b[?1003l\x1b[?1006l\x1b[?2004l\x1b[<u\x1b[>4;0m`
   (reset attributes, show cursor, disable mouse tracking ×4, disable bracketed paste, reset modifyCursorKeys, reset modifyOtherKeys)

**Proof 1 — logs --follow fatal error path** (full terminal output):
```
$ openclaw logs --follow --url ws://127.0.0.1:18789
[agent-scope] Multiple agents marked default=true; using the first entry as default.

◇  Config warnings ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  - plugins.entries.voice-call: plugin disabled ...         │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
Gateway not reachable. Is it running and accessible?
Gateway target: ws://127.0.0.1:18789
Source: cli --url
Config: /home/0668000452/.openclaw/openclaw.json
Hint: run `openclaw doctor`.
←─ RESET_SEQUENCE emitted here (see hex evidence below)
>>> exit code: 1
```

**Proof 2 — hooks enable error path** (full terminal output):
```
$ openclaw hooks enable nonexistent-hook
[agent-scope] Multiple agents marked default=true; using the first entry as default.

◇  Config warnings ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  - plugins.entries.voice-call: plugin disabled ...         │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
Error: Hook "nonexistent-hook" not found
←─ RESET_SEQUENCE emitted here (see hex evidence below)
>>> exit code: 1
```

**ANSI reset sequence hex evidence** (extracted from both command outputs):

Both error paths emit the identical ANSI reset sequence after the error message:
```
ESC[0m        ← reset all SGR attributes (colors, bold, etc.)
ESC[?25h      ← show cursor (DECTCEM)
ESC[?1000l    ← disable basic mouse tracking
ESC[?1002l    ← disable button-event mouse tracking
ESC[?1003l    ← disable any-event mouse tracking
ESC[?1006l    ← disable SGR mouse mode
ESC[?2004l    ← disable bracketed paste mode
ESC[<u        ← reset modifyCursorKeys
ESC[>4;0m     ← reset modifyOtherKeys
```

This sequence matches the `RESET_SEQUENCE` constant in `packages/terminal-core/src/restore.ts` exactly, proving `restoreTerminalState()` was called.

**Exit code verification**: Both commands exit with code `1` (from `defaultRuntime.exit(1)` → `process.exit(1)`), not timeout (124).

**Terminal function verification**: After exit, `tput cols` (80 columns), `tput cnorm` (show cursor), and `tput setaf` (color output) all work correctly, confirming terminal state is restored.

### What Was Not Tested

- `hooks relay` command error path (requires a running agent session)
- `hooks install` / `hooks update` error paths (require plugin registry)
- TTY with raw mode previously set by Node.js `setRawMode(true)` — shell `stty raw` is not tracked by libuv, so `setRawMode(false)` is a no-op in this test. However, all operations in `restoreTerminalState()` have TTY guards and try/catch, and `process.stdout.write(RESET_SEQUENCE)` is idempotent. The ANSI reset sequence is emitted regardless, which is the primary defense against terminal state corruption.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/cli/hooks-cli.ts` | Add `throw new Error("unreachable")` after `defaultRuntime.exit(1)` to preserve `never` type contract |
| `src/cli/logs-cli.ts` | Replace manual `restoreTerminalState` + `process.exit(1)` with canonical `defaultRuntime.exit(1)` |
| `src/cli/logs-cli.test.ts` | Add `vi.mock("../runtime.js")` to prevent runtime's unreachable throw from escaping when tests mock `process.exit` |

target.title: fix(memory): re-throw non-ENOENT/ENOTDIR errors in root memory file lookup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveCanonicalRootMemoryFile` uses an empty `catch {}` when calling `fs.readdir` on the workspace directory. This swallows all errors, including `EACCES` (permission denied). When a workspace directory exists but is not readable, the function returns `null` — making the root memory file silently disappear. Agents then operate without their context with no error signal.

## Why This Change Was Made

Only `ENOENT` (directory does not exist) and `ENOTDIR` (path is not a directory) should return `null`. All other errors — especially `EACCES` — should propagate so the caller can report or handle the problem. This matches the error-handling pattern used elsewhere in the codebase (e.g., `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts`).

## Evidence

Added test file `src/memory/root-memory-files.test.ts` with 4 cases:
- Non-existent directory (ENOENT) → returns null ✓
- Empty directory → returns null ✓
- Directory with MEMORY.md → returns correct path ✓

target.title: fix(whatsapp): normalize hosted JIDs consistently with Baileys
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where WhatsApp hosted identities could be accepted by ingress classification but rejected or compared differently by target normalization, allowlists, mentions, approvals, and quoted-message lookup.

The WhatsApp plugin had several independent JID parsers with different supported-domain sets. In particular, some paths recognized `hosted` and `hosted.lid`, while others only recognized `s.whatsapp.net`, `c.us`, and `lid`. Device-qualified JIDs and PN/LID comparisons were also normalized independently across these paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds one typed WhatsApp JID module backed by Baileys' shipped JID parser, encoder, normalizer, and domain classifiers. Target normalization, runtime resolution, comparable identities, inbound classification, mentions, approval authorization, quote lookup, and PN/LID mapping now consume that canonical classification.

WhatsApp application policy remains explicit above the protocol layer: target prefixes and E.164 allowlist rules stay plugin-owned, and PN-to-LID equivalence still requires the mapping store. The implementation deliberately does not use Baileys' `areJidsSameUser`, because comparing only the user component could equate unrelated PN and LID identities.

The change is confined to `extensions/whatsapp/src/**`; it does not change core or Plugin SDK contracts. It adds no compatibility shim, fallback parser, config surface, or storage path.

## User Impact

WhatsApp hosted PN/LID identities and device-qualified JIDs are now interpreted consistently across inbound and outbound flows. Operators can expect target validation, E.164 allowlists, approval authorization, mentions, quote matching, and stored PN/LID mappings to follow the same domain and canonicalization rules.

Malformed or unsupported identities fail closed, and same-digit PN/LID identities are not treated as equal without an explicit mapping.

## Evidence

- `pnpm check:changed`: passed, including extension production/test typechecks, formatting, lint, structural guards, and runtime import-cycle checks.

target.title: fix(gateway): remove non-null assertion in createTimeoutRace shutdown helper
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `createTimeoutRace` helper in `src/gateway/server-close.ts` uses a `let resolve!` non-null assertion that TypeScript cannot verify. The `resolve` variable is assigned inside a Promise constructor (which runs synchronously) but lives outside it, requiring the `!` suffix to satisfy the compiler. This is a code smell listed in issue #106645 — the self-clearing timer coupled with a detached resolve binding is fragile and would break if the function were refactored to an async context.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix moves the `setTimeout` into the Promise executor, making `resolve` a native Promise constructor parameter. This eliminates the non-null assertion entirely and makes the code self-documenting: the timer lifecycle is now visibly scoped to the promise it controls.

## Evidence

- **Existing tests**: `src/gateway/server-close.test.ts` — 43/43 passing (indirect coverage through the public shutdown API that uses `createTimeoutRace`)
- **Behavioral equivalence**: The Promise executor runs synchronously per spec (ECMA-262), so `timer` is still assigned before the function returns. The `clear()` method cancels the timer identically to before. All 7 call sites use the same `Promise.race` + `clear()` pattern and are unaffected.

## Merge Risk

Low — purely internal refactor, same public API surface, all existing tests pass.

Fixes #106645

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before the original implementation:

```text
expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times
```

Exact CI repair reproduction on failed head `166b22c`, against event base `6d31c16`:

```text

TypeScript LOC ratchet failed: oversized legacy files may not grow.
```

The repaired committed tree passes the same exact-base ratchet and leaves the file at 1229 lines versus 1230 on the base. Complete affected test files also pass:

```text

Gateway call wrapper:     119 passed (119)
```

Real behavior proof used an isolated OpenClaw Gateway and the production `callGateway -> GatewayClient -> GatewayProtocolClient` path for an authenticated `health` RPC over a real loopback WebSocket:

```text

Callback ran before response resolution: true
Callback intentionally threw: yes
Request still resolved successfully: yes
```

The send-exception regression also verifies that `onDispatched` is not called when `socket.send` fails and that pending request state is cleaned up.

Repository and package gates:

```text

Scoped lint: passed
Scoped formatting: passed for all 6 changed files
```

On the failed head, hosted `check-prod-types` and `check-test-types` both passed; the only primary code failure was the LOC ratchet, with `openclaw/ci-gate` failing as its aggregate. Updated hosted CI will rerun those lanes on the repaired head.

target.title: fix(shared): re-throw non-ENOENT errors in ignore-rules file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`addIgnoreRules` uses an empty `catch {}` when reading `.gitignore`/`.ignore`/`.fdignore` files. This swallows **all** errors, including `EACCES` (permission denied). When a file exists but is unreadable due to permissions, the ignore rules are silently skipped, causing files that should be ignored to appear in scan results — a false-negative security issue.

## Why This Change Was Made

Only `ENOENT` (file disappeared between `existsSync` and `readFileSync`) should be silently ignored. All other errors — especially `EACCES`, `EISDIR`, encoding errors — should propagate so callers can react appropriately.

Closes #98968
Related: #98992

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators relying on diagnostics would see incomplete token and cost totals when plugins call `runtime.llm.complete`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The host runtime now emits one trusted `model.usage` event after a successful plugin completion when diagnostics are enabled and usage is nonzero. Attribution uses the trusted plugin policy owner, so request-shaped caller data and nested plugin scopes cannot relabel telemetry.

The OTel and Prometheus exporters expose the bounded plugin owner on their OpenClaw usage metrics. Non-plugin events use `none`, keeping each metric's label set stable, while the plugin SDK completion result remains unchanged. Plugin completion latency is deliberately not mapped to `openclaw.run.duration_ms`; that histogram remains agent-run only. This follows the implementation direction from #98992; its author is credited in the commit trailer.

## User Impact

Operators can now account for tokens and cost from plugin-initiated LLM calls in the same dashboards and traces as main agent usage. Existing non-plugin usage series gain the explicit `plugin="none"` / `openclaw.plugin="none"` attribute. Plugin call latency does not alter the existing agent-run duration metric.

target.title: fix(skills): enforce byte-level cap on skill package downloads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where skill package downloads via `pipeline(response.body, file)` have no byte-level cap. A malicious or compromised ClawHub registry could return an oversized response with missing or large Content-Length and fill the disk before the `timeoutMs` guard fires.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add two layers of protection, scoped to OpenClaw-managed skill sources (openclaw-bundled, openclaw-managed, openclaw-extra):

1. **Content-Length pre-check**: If the response declares a Content-Length exceeding 256 MB, reject immediately without streaming any bytes. The response body is cancelled before throwing.
2. **Streaming byte counter**: A `Transform` callback tracks cumulative bytes during the pipeline. If 256 MB is exceeded mid-stream (e.g. chunked transfer encoding with no Content-Length), the transform calls `callback(error)`, meaning the boundary-crossing chunk **never reaches the file**.

**Scope narrowing**: The byte cap only applies to skill installs from OpenClaw-managed sources. Custom/workspace skill downloads (skillSource=unknown/user) are unrestricted for backward compatibility. This addresses the ClawSweeper compatibility concern — existing >256 MB downloads from custom sources continue to work.

256 MB was chosen to match the magnitude of `LOCAL_SKILL_CARD_MAX_BYTES` naming style from the same module.

## User Impact

None under normal operation. Legitimate skill packages from managed registries (typically <50 MB) are unaffected. Oversized downloads are rejected with a clear error message. Custom skill downloads with large artifacts (>256 MB) are not affected.

## Evidence

### Automated tests — 11 tests passed

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  11 passed (11)
 Type Errors  no errors
 Lint         no errors
```

Test coverage includes:
- **Content-Length path**: Real HTTP loopback server returning `content-length: 536870912` → download rejected with `exceeds maximum allowed`
- **Chunked streaming path**: Mocked 320 MB stream (5 × 64 MB chunks) over chunked transfer → rejected at 256 MB boundary, crossing chunk never written to disk
- **Compat path (no maxBytes)**: Both Content-Length and chunked scenarios verified to succeed when `maxBytes` is omitted
- **Response cancellation**: Failed/cancelled response bodies are cancelled before error propagation (non-ok path + oversized Content-Length path)
- All pre-existing safety tests (path traversal, symlink, preflight change detection) continue to pass

### ClawSweeper findings resolved

| Finding | Status |
|---------|--------|
| Cancel oversized response body before throwing | ✅ Fixed — `cancelIgnoredResponseBody(response)` called before Content-Length rejection |
| Compatibility contract (256 MB global limit) | ✅ Addressed — cap scoped to OpenClaw-managed sources only |
| Integrated real behavior proof | ✅ Tests exercise `installDownloadSpec` directly through the real code path |

### Codex review remediation

The first implementation used `PassThrough.on("data")` which detected overflow **after** the boundary-crossing chunk had already been forwarded to the write stream. Changed to `Transform._transform(chunk, encoding, callback)` where `callback(error)` prevents the chunk from reaching the file. Added a chunked streaming overflow test to cover the undeclared-length path.

---

AI-assisted.

With the official Codex plugin enabled, a typo like `openclaw stats --deep` previously printed:

- Register Codex CLI descriptors first so they stay discoverable in every load mode.
- Gate full runtime wiring (binding store, harness, providers, tools, hooks) on `api.registrationMode !== "full"`, matching `extensions/copilot` / `extensions/openshell` and the plugin SDK entrypoint contract.
- Regression coverage for all non-full modes with an empty runtime: `cli-metadata`, `discovery`, `tool-discovery`, `setup-only`, `setup-runtime`.

However, investigation found no code path where Braille characters alone would cause this behavior—the markdown-it image renderer only accepts `data:image/...;base64,` URLs, not arbitrary text with Braille characters.

## Why This Change Was Made

target.title: perf(agents): scope subagent registry reads

## What Problem This Solves

Controller-scoped subagent reads were hydrating the entire persisted registry. The original PR #105489 also missed a replacement-write cache invalidation path and carried unrelated history. This clean replacement uses indexed controller and child-session reads so the control, abort, and gateway follow-up paths do not immediately fall back to full hydration.

## Why This Change Was Made

SQLite already has controller, requester, and child-session indexes. The store now owns the scoped predicates; state owns a bounded 500 ms, 64-entry process-local cache; registry accessors retain the existing controller/requester fallback and latest-generation semantics. Successful writes invalidate every scoped cache entry, including the throwing persistence path.

## User Impact

Large registries no longer need to be fully loaded for controller list, child latest, or display lookups. Existing JSON-to-SQLite migration, in-memory active/ended precedence, and broad tree/index APIs are preserved.

## Evidence

- Local portable Node v24.15.0 focused tests: store 6/6, state 12/12, read accessor 1/1, registry 110/110.
- TDD RED/GREEN coverage includes controller/requester fallback, child generation, legacy migration, scoped cache TTL/cap/namespace/invalidation, replacement-write invalidation, and guards against full-snapshot accessor use.
- Independent per-task and final full-branch reviews approved the resulting diff.
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` is clean; the branch contains only eight intended registry source/test files across four commits.

## Proof gaps

## What Problem This Solves

`runSandboxHttpRequest` in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/http.ts` parsed the sandbox shell helper's stdout with an unguarded `JSON.parse`. When the helper exits 0 but emits non-JSON output, the raw `SyntaxError` can include the helper output and is returned through the exec-server JSON-RPC error boundary without identifying `sandbox http/request`.

## Why This Change Was Made

target.title: fix(memory): backfill provider.model with resolved model name
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a memory embedding adapter returns an empty `provider.model` (because the user did not explicitly configure a model, leaving it to `adapter.defaultModel`), the downstream memory identity, `providerKey`, chunk model tags, and vector search filters all see `""` instead of the resolved model name. This causes persistent `Dirty` index state and broken vector search (`WHERE c.model = ''` returns zero rows), reported as issue #90042.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `createWithAdapter` function already resolves the model via `resolveProviderModel(adapter, options.model)` and passes it into `adapter.create(...)`. But the returned `result.provider.model` can be empty if the adapter itself returns an empty string — the resolved model is discarded after `create` returns, leaving downstream consumers with no fallback.

The fix is a property assignment backfill at the return site in `createWithAdapter`: if `result.provider` exists but `result.provider.model` is falsy, assign the resolved model. This is a *runtime backfill*, not a persisted-data migration.

## Behavior Matrix

| Scenario | result.provider.model | adapter.defaultModel (resolvedModel) | Before | After | Changed? |
|----------|----------------------|--------------------------------------|--------|-------|----------|
| User explicitly sets model | `"qwen3-8b"` | irrelevant | `"qwen3-8b"` | `"qwen3-8b"` | ❌ No |
| User leaves empty, adapter has default | `""` | `"text-embedding-3-small"` | `""` (bug) | `"text-embedding-3-small"` | ✅ Fix |
| User leaves empty, adapter has no default | `""` | `""` | `""` | `""` | ❌ No |
| User leaves empty, provider returns correct model | `"ada-002"` | irrelevant | `"ada-002"` | `"ada-002"` | ❌ No |

Only scenario 2 changes, which is the exact bug from issue #90042.

## User Impact

Transparent for correct configurations (scenarios 1, 3, 4 — zero change). Users who saw a persistent `Dirty` index due to an empty `provider.model` will find their vector search working again after upgrade. No migration or reindex needed for new indexes; existing dirty indexes require a one-time `openclaw memory status --index`.

## Evidence

### Code Evidence

`extensions/memory-core/src/memory/embeddings.ts:245-247`:
```ts
if (result.provider && !result.provider.model) {
  result.provider.model = createOptions.model;
}
```

Direct property assignment (not spread operator) so prototype methods on the provider object are preserved. Regression test at `embeddings.test.ts:350-370`.

### Real Behavior Proof

**Behavior addressed**: `provider.model` is empty when the adapter returns no model, causing identity mis-match and persistent dirty index.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node v24.18.0, branch `fix/provider-model-backfill-90042-reborn`, commit 03f60bc022.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
pnpm openclaw memory status --deep
```

**Evidence after fix**:
```
Memory Search (main)
Provider: openai (requested: openai)
Model: Qwen3-Embedding-8B
Sources: memory
Indexed: 50/131 files · 697 chunks
Dirty: yes
Store: ~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
Embeddings: ready
Index identity: index was built for model fts-only, expected Qwen3-Embedding-8B
Vector search: paused until memory is rebuilt
Fix: Run: openclaw memory status --index --agent main
```

Key observations:
1. **`Model: Qwen3-Embedding-8B`** — The backfill works. `provider.model` carries the resolved model name, not `""`.
2. **`expected Qwen3-Embedding-8B`** — The identity check at `manager-reindex-state.ts:145` now receives a proper model.
3. **`index was built for model fts-only`** — This is the *existing dirty index* created before this patch, proving the bug existed.
4. The identity flow (`this.provider.model` → `resolveMemoryIndexIdentityState` → `expectedModel`) executes the same code path as every restart. With this PR, fresh indexes will store the correct model and remain clean.

**Observed result after fix**: After a one-time reindex, the new `meta.model` will match `expectedModel` and the index is clean. Without this fix, `expectedModel` stays `fts-only` and the index stays dirty forever.

**What was not tested**: Full reindex (`openclaw memory status --index`) on this workspace — blocked by a local `sqlite-vec` native extension load issue unrelated to the PR logic. The identity validation code path (`resolveMemoryIndexIdentityState`) is proven correct by the `expected Qwen3-Embedding-8B` output above, which is the exact function called on every gateway restart.

## Regression Test Plan

| Test file | What it covers | Why minimal |
|-----------|---------------|-------------|
| `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/embeddings.test.ts` | 3 scenarios: explicit model preserves value, empty model backfills, provider with correct model unchanged | Direct coverage of the changed function |
| `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/generic-embedding-provider.bridge.test.ts` | `createEmbeddingProvider` + identity round-trip | Covers the call site in the bridge path |

target.title: fix(agents): preserve yielded subagent continuations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A required-completion subagent can end a turn with `sessions_yield` while waiting for an external continuation. The embedded runner already returns `yielded: true` with `livenessState: "paused"`, but the deferred success lifecycle emitted by `agent-command` dropped those terminal fields. The subagent registry therefore observed a normal successful end, finalized the tracked run, and started a requester announce before the real continuation arrived.

Plugin-owned follow-up runs on the same child session also registered a new best-effort subagent row before the existing ended row could be reactivated. That hid the original required-completion routing from the existing continuation mechanism.

This addresses the `sessions_yield` premature-finalization path reported in #101862. It does not address the sibling case where an orchestrator emits ordinary intermediate text instead of yielding.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Use one terminal lifecycle projection for both successful and error results, preserving `stopReason`, liveness, timeout attribution, replay state, and `yielded`.
- Reactivate an ended/yielded tracked subagent run before registering a new plugin-owned run for the same child session.
- Prepare that tracking only after the accepted run passes the queue-abort check, avoiding replacement records for runs that never dispatch.
- Reuse the existing `replaceSubagentRunAfterSteer` continuation path instead of adding a new plugin SDK or protocol surface.

## User Impact

When a spawned subagent calls `sessions_yield`, its tracked run remains paused and no premature parent announce is started. A later plugin follow-up on the same child session inherits the original requester/completion route, and the parent is announced only after that continuation genuinely completes.

No configuration, migration, or public SDK change is required.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(plugins): handle NaN from Date.parse in catalog rollback detection
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`isHostedCatalogSignedFeedRollback` uses `Date.parse()` to compare `generatedAt` timestamps but never checks for `NaN`. When `generatedAt` contains an invalid date string, `Date.parse` returns `NaN`, and `NaN < validNumber` evaluates to `false` — meaning an invalid candidate is silently accepted as newer rather than being treated as a potential rollback.

This is a safety issue: a corrupted or tampered feed with an invalid `generatedAt` could bypass the rollback guard.

## Why This Change Was Made

- If the **candidate** has an invalid `generatedAt`, we conservatively treat it as a rollback (reject it).
- If the **current** feed has an invalid `generatedAt`, we treat the candidate as not a rollback (accept it).
- This follows the principle of least surprise: invalid data in the incoming feed should not silently bypass safety checks.

## Evidence

Added 5 unit tests for `isHostedCatalogSignedFeedRollback` (via `__testing` export):
- Candidate newer by sequence → not rollback ✓
- Candidate older by sequence → rollback ✓
- Equal sequence, candidate older date → rollback ✓
- Equal sequence, **candidate has invalid date** → rollback ✓
- Equal sequence, **current has invalid date** → not rollback ✓

## Summary

Native hook descriptors were not regenerated when the relay was unavailable during gateway restart, causing hooks to silently fail until manual intervention. Falls through to normal OpenClaw policy evaluation instead of hard-blocking when the relay is unavailable.

## Linked context

Closes #89325

## Real behavior proof

- Real environment tested: Codex app-server with native hook relay (unit/integration tests)
- Exact steps or command run after this patch (rebased onto origin/main, 2026-07-16):
```
vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.cli.config.ts \
    src/cli/native-hook-relay-cli.test.ts
```
- Evidence after fix: CLI-level native hook tests pass; fallthrough behavior confirmed
- Observed result after fix: Relay unavailability triggers fallthrough to policy evaluation instead of hard-block
- Rebase status: Rebased onto latest origin/main (fdd1acb3285), no conflicts
- What was not tested: Live relay restart cycle on real Codex harness
- Proof limitations or environment constraints: Relay lifecycle testing requires live Codex; unit tests cover the code path

## Tests and validation

- Commands: `vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.cli.config.ts`
- Regression coverage: approval-bridge.test.ts covers both error and fallthrough paths
- Before: Relay unavailable at restart → native hook descriptors not regenerated → hooks silently fail
